narrative:
The model estimated a 71.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—meaning that, among students with a similar profile, roughly seven in ten would be expected to fail. Because the school used this prediction in its admission decision, your application was rejected.

The strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure was your first-year class rank. You were in the second decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. The second-most important factor was your third-year class rank: you were in the third decile, compared with an accepted-student average of about 5.8. Both signals suggested weaker academic standing than the model associated with bar-exam success. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.80, versus an accepted-student average of 3.23, was the third most influential factor and also pushed toward failure. These three academic indicators were the main reasons the model leaned toward failure rather than passing.

To strengthen a future application, ask admissions or an academic advisor for specific feedback, consider retaking the LSAT if you can improve your score, and take additional rigorous coursework that demonstrates readiness for law study. If prior grades were affected by circumstances, document that context. Build a concrete bar-exam preparation plan and reapply when your record gives stronger evidence that you can succeed.
